input: Can I work while studying in Finland? How many hours?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'working-and-internships-during-studies or right-to-work', and mentions 30 and week.
actual_result:
- Yes, you can work while studying in Finland.
- The average working hours can be up to 30 hours per week.
- This limit can be exceeded in some weeks, as long as the yearly average remains at 30 hours per week.
- For EU/EEA citizens, there are no restrictions on working.
- For non-EU citizens, you can work part-time for up to 30 hours per week, or full-time if writing a thesis or completing practical training related to your degree. [2][1]

input: Can I work full-time during the summer holidays?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'working-and-internships-during-studies or right-to-work', and mentions holiday and full-time/full time.
actual_result: - Yes, you can work full-time during summer holidays, provided that your average working hours do not exceed 30 hours per week at the end of the year. [1]

input: Does an internship that is part of my degree count towards the 30-hour work limit?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'working-and-internships-during-studies', and mentions internship and not/does not/doesn't.
actual_result:
- If the internship is part of your degree and has been agreed upon as such, it does not count towards the 30-hour work limit [1].
- If the internship is registered as part of your studies, the 30-hour limit will apply [1].

input: How much money do I need per month for a student residence permit?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'income-requirement-for-students or instructions-for-degree-students or instructions-for-exchange-students', and mentions 800.
actual_result:
- For a student residence permit, you need to have at least 800 euros per month available for living expenses [1][3].

- If you are applying for an extended permit for a period shorter than 1 year, you will need to have 800 euros per month at your disposal [3].

- For studies lasting 1 year or longer, you must have EUR 9,600 in your bank account when you submit the application [1][2].

input: My studies last more than one year. How much money must I have in my bank account when I apply?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'income-requirement-for-students', and mentions 9,600/9600/9 600.
actual_result:
- You must have EUR 9,600 in your bank account when you submit the application. [1]

- If you have received a grant or scholarship, subtract the amount from EUR 9,600. For example, if you have a grant of EUR 2,000, you need to have EUR 7,600 in your bank account. [1]

- Ensure your bank statement includes the name of the account holder, the bank name, and the currency. [1]

input: What health insurance do I need for a student residence permit if my studies last less than two years?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'insurance or instructions-for-degree-students or instructions-for-exchange-students', and mentions 120,000/120 000/120000.
actual_result:
- You need health insurance that covers medical expenses up to EUR 120,000.
- This insurance can be taken out from an insurance company in your home country or an international insurance company.
- Examples of suitable insurance providers include:
  - Assurances Courtages et Services (ACS) (www.acs-ami.com)
  - Aon Student Insurance (www.aonstudentinsurance.com)
  - International Student Insurance (www.internationalstudentinsurance.com)
  - Swisscare – ESI Finland plan (https://swisscare.com/)

[1]

input: How many study credits do I need per year to get an extended residence permit for studies?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'extended-permit-for-studies or instructions-for-students-applying-for-an-extended-permit', and mentions 45.
actual_result:
- You need to complete at least 45 credits during an academic year to avoid being refused a residence permit [1].

If you have completed fewer credits, you must provide a statement explaining the reasons for not making enough progress in your studies [1].

input: Do I have to be in Finland to receive the decision on my extended permit?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'extended-permit-for-studies or residence-permit-extension', and mentions finland.
actual_result: Yes, you must be in Finland to receive the decision on your extended permit [1].

input: Can I keep working while my extended permit application is being processed?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'working-while-your-extended-permit-application-is-being-processed', and mentions work.
actual_result:
- You can usually continue working under your current permit while your application for an extended permit is being processed, provided you apply before your current permit expires [1].

- If you apply after your current permit has expired, you may not be allowed to continue working on that basis [1].

- For seasonal workers, refer to specific guidance on continuing to work [1].

- If your application is denied, your right to work may continue until a deportation decision is enforceable or until an administrative court decision [1].

- For permits in national labour shortage sectors, you can start working immediately and continue during the application process if you apply before your current permit expires [1].

input: How do I get a Finnish personal identity code?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'personal-identity-code or foreigner-registration', and mentions identity code.
actual_result:
To get a Finnish personal identity code, follow these steps:

- **If you are a foreign student**: You need a residence permit to get a personal identity code. Once you have a residence permit, you can request a personal identity code. The processing time is 2-3 weeks for work or study purposes, and 3-4 weeks for other reasons [1][2].

- **If you are a child born in Finland**: Your parents need not take any measures. The hospital will register your birth and issue a personal identity code.

- **If you are a child adopted to Finland**: You will usually receive a personal identity code after arriving in Finland, but in some cases, you might get one before entering the country [1].

- **If you are a Finnish citizen born abroad**: You can request a personal identity code after the Digital and Population Data Services Agency registers you in the Population Information System [1].

The process is free of charge [2].

input: After submitting the personal identity code form to DVV, how soon must I visit them?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'foreigner-registration', and mentions 1 month/one month.
actual_result: - You must visit the Digital and Population Data Services Agency within 1 month of submitting the form to request a personal identity code [1].

input: How do I get a tax card in Finland?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'tax_card or tax-card or Studying-in-Finland or work_in_finland', and mentions tax card.
actual_result:
To get a tax card in Finland, follow these steps:

- Register as a resident with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency to obtain a Finnish personal identity code [1][2].
- Go to a Tax Administration service point to apply for a tax card. You may also apply through the MyTax online service or by phone [1][2].

If you need to work immediately, be aware that service points might not be able to issue a tax card right away. The processing time is usually 1 to 3 business days [2].

input: What is the tax at source rate for a student staying in Finland temporarily?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'Studying-in-Finland', and mentions 35.
actual_result:
- For non-residents, the tax at source rate is 35% [1].

This rate applies if you are staying in Finland temporarily and are considered a non-resident taxpayer. Your wages will be taxed at this rate after the tax-at-source deduction of €510 per month or €17 per day [1].

input: How much must I earn per month from work in Finland to get Kela benefits?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'kela.fi', and mentions 800.
actual_result: - You must earn at least EUR 800.02 per month from work in Finland to get Kela benefits. [1][2]

input: What is a Kela card and how do I get one?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'kela-card', and mentions kela card.
actual_result:
- A Kela card proves your right to Kela reimbursements for health insurance.
- You usually don't need to show the card, as your right can be checked electronically with ID.
- You need the card if you visit a private doctor or dentist who cannot check your information electronically.
- Kela sends the card automatically to those covered by the Finnish national health insurance scheme and newborn children.
- To get a Kela card, use OmaKela e-service if available, or fill out a form and send it to Kela.
- No fee is charged for renewal.
- If you lose your card, apply for a new one through OmaKela or by filling out a form and sending it to Kela. [1]

input: Can I stay in Finland to look for work after I graduate?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'after-graduation or seeking-work-after-graduation or residence-permit-extension', and mentions work.
actual_result:
- Yes, you can apply for a residence permit to look for work after graduation if you have a residence permit for studies or research and do not yet have a job or do not earn enough to qualify for a work-based residence permit [1][3].

- If you are a citizen of an EU, EEA, or Swiss country, you have the right to work in Finland without limitations during your studies [2].

- If you are from another country, you can work part-time (up to 30 hours a week) or full-time if you are writing your thesis or completing practical training related to your degree [2].

- Ensure you maintain valid insurance coverage for the duration of your stay in Finland [2].

input: Can my spouse and children come to Finland with me while I study?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'students-family-members', and mentions family.
actual_result:
- Yes, your spouse and children can come to Finland with you if you are granted a residence permit for studies [1][2].
- They will need to apply for a residence permit based on family ties [1][2].
- Note that the processing of family members' applications may not happen at the same time as yours [2].

input: Do I need a residence permit to study in Finland?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'right-of-residence or eu-citizen', and mentions regist. Answer is tailored to the user profile.
actual_result:
- If you are an EU/EEA or Nordic citizen, you do not need a residence permit to study in Finland [1].
- However, you still need to register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) within 14 days of arrival [1].
- For non-EU/EEA citizens, you may need a residence permit for studies, depending on the type of degree program [1].
- Check the specific requirements for your program on the Migri website [1].

input: Do I need a residence permit to study in Finland?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'migri.fi', and mentions residence permit. Answer is tailored to the user profile.
actual_result:
- Yes, you need a residence permit for studies in Finland if your studies take longer than 90 days [1].
- As a non-EU citizen, you must apply for a residence permit even if your studies are longer than 90 days [1].
- The type of residence permit (A or B) depends on whether your studies lead to a degree or not [1].

input: How much money do I need to show for my permit?
expected_behavior: Answers from official sources, cites a page matching 'income-requirement-for-students or instructions-for-exchange-students', and mentions 800. Answer is tailored to the user profile.
actual_result:
- As a non-EU exchange student with a planned stay of less than 1 year, you need to show 800 euros per month at your disposal [1][2].

- You must have 9,600 euros on your bank account when you submit the application [1].

- If your educational institution supports your living in Finland, you may not need to show 800 euros per month [1].

- Attach bank statements showing the required amount and include the name of the account holder, account number, balance, and currency [2].
